title.en: Section 1 - Enrolling for a Music Course
title.zh: 第一部分 - 报名音乐课程

sections.passage:
A woman calls the Community Music School to enroll in a piano course. The administrator, Andrew, answers the call and helps her through the registration process.

Andrew welcomes the caller and asks about her musical background. The woman explains that she played the piano as a child, reaching Grade 5, but stopped when she went to university about fifteen years ago. She now wants to restart her playing and feels she needs structured lessons to get back to her previous standard.

Andrew describes the available piano courses. The Beginner course is for those with no prior experience and runs on Monday evenings from 7 to 9 PM. The Intermediate course, suitable for those with Grades 3 to 5, runs on Wednesday evenings from 7 to 9 PM. The Advanced course for Grade 6 and above runs on Thursday evenings. Based on her background, Andrew recommends the Intermediate course, though the woman could also consider the Advanced course if she progresses quickly after a few weeks of practice.

The course runs for twelve weeks, from September 6th to November 22nd, with a one-week break during the half-term holiday in late October. The fee is 180 pounds for the full course, or 65 pounds per month if she prefers to pay in installments. There is also a registration fee of 15 pounds which covers the cost of course materials and music books.

The school provides pianos for all students during lessons, but Andrew recommends that she practice at home between sessions. If she does not have a piano, the school has practice rooms available for booking at 5 pounds per hour. These rooms each contain a well-maintained upright piano and are available from 9 AM to 9 PM on weekdays and from 10 AM to 6 PM on weekends.

Andrew asks for her personal details to complete the registration. Her name is Catherine Walsh, and she lives at 14 Maple Drive. Her phone number is 07845 239167 and her email is c.walsh@email.com. Andrew confirms that she will receive a confirmation email within 24 hours with all the course details and a list of what to bring to the first lesson.

title.en: Section 2 - Tour of a New Leisure Complex
title.zh: 第二部分 - 参观新的休闲中心

sections.passage:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the grand opening of the Meadowbrook Leisure Complex. My name is Victoria, and I'll be showing you around our new facilities today. This complex has been three years in the planning and eighteen months in construction, and we're very proud of the result.

The complex is built on the site of the former Meadowbrook factory, which closed in 2015. The developers have retained the original Victorian brick facade of the main building, which dates back to 1890, and have created a modern interior that complements the historic exterior. The total investment in the project has been 45 million pounds.

The centerpiece of the complex is our 50-meter Olympic-standard swimming pool, which has a movable floor that can be adjusted to different depths for different activities. It's suitable for competitive swimming, water polo, and recreational use. There's also a separate teaching pool for children and beginners, and a diving pool with platforms at 3, 5, 7.5, and 10 meters. The aquatic center can accommodate up to 500 spectators for swimming competitions.

The sports hall is one of the largest in the region, with 12 badminton courts, a full-size basketball court, and seating for 800 people. It's available for hire by sports clubs, schools, and community groups, and we've already had bookings from several local leagues. The hall is also equipped with a retractable stage for performances and events.

Our fitness center occupies the entire second floor and includes over 200 pieces of state-of-the-art exercise equipment, a spin studio with 40 bikes, and three exercise studios for classes ranging from yoga and pilates to high-intensity interval training. Personal training services are available at 40 pounds per session or 350 pounds for a package of ten sessions.

For families, we have a children's adventure play area covering 500 square meters, with equipment suitable for children aged 2 to 12. There's also a soft play area for toddlers under 3. Parents can relax in our family cafe, which has a viewing window overlooking the play area.

The complex opens to the public this Saturday, and we're offering a special introductory membership rate. Individual annual membership is 400 pounds, a saving of 100 pounds on the standard price. Family membership for two adults and up to three children is 700 pounds, a saving of 150 pounds. These special rates are available until the end of the month.

title.en: Section 3 - Discussion Between a Student and Tutor About an Assignment
title.zh: 第三部分 - 学生和导师关于作业的讨论

sections.passage:
Tomoko, a postgraduate student in Business Studies, meets her tutor Dr. Fisher to discuss her dissertation research on customer loyalty programs in the airline industry.

Dr. Fisher asks Tomoko about her progress. She explains that she has completed her literature review and is now designing her research methodology. She initially planned to use only a quantitative approach, conducting an online survey of 500 frequent flyers. However, after reading several methodological papers, she has decided to adopt a mixed-methods approach that combines quantitative and qualitative data.

For the quantitative component, Tomoko plans to survey frequent flyers who are members of at least two different airline loyalty programs. She will distribute the survey through online forums and social media groups dedicated to frequent travelers. The survey will use a 7-point Likert scale to measure customer satisfaction, perceived value, brand loyalty, and intention to continue membership. She aims to collect at least 300 valid responses.

For the qualitative component, she plans to conduct semi-structured interviews with 15 frequent flyers who have been members of loyalty programs for at least five years. She wants to explore the emotional and psychological factors that influence loyalty beyond what can be captured in a survey. The interviews will last approximately 45 minutes each and will be recorded with participants' consent.

Dr. Fisher approves of the mixed-methods approach but raises several concerns. First, she worries about sampling bias in the online survey, as the respondents may not be representative of all frequent flyers. Tomoko acknowledges this limitation but argues that online recruitment is the most practical way to access this specific population. Second, Dr. Fisher suggests that Tomoko should consider including a comparative element, perhaps contrasting loyalty programs from a full-service carrier with those from a low-cost carrier, to add depth to her analysis.

They discuss the timeline for completing the research. Tomoko plans to pilot her survey in the first week of February, make any necessary revisions, and then launch the full survey in mid-February. She hopes to complete data collection by the end of March, leaving April and May for analysis and writing. The dissertation deadline is June 15th. Dr. Fisher recommends that Tomoko start writing her methodology chapter now while the details are fresh in her mind, rather than waiting until all data is collected.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on the Psychology of Color in Marketing
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于营销中色彩心理学的讲座

sections.passage:
Good afternoon. Today's lecture examines how color influences consumer behavior and the ways in which marketers exploit our psychological responses to different colors to sell products and build brands. This is a topic that sits at the intersection of psychology, neuroscience, and marketing, and it has profound implications for how companies design everything from packaging to retail environments.

The relationship between color and emotion has been studied for over a century. Research consistently shows that colors evoke specific emotional and physiological responses. Red, for example, increases heart rate and creates a sense of urgency, which is why it is commonly used in sale signs and clearance tags. Blue conveys trust and reliability, making it the most popular color for financial institutions and technology companies. Think about how many banks use blue in their logos: Barclays, Deutsche Bank, American Express, and PayPal, to name just a few.

Green is associated with nature, health, and wealth. Organic and environmentally friendly brands frequently use green in their branding to signal their commitment to sustainability. Whole Foods Market, for example, uses a predominantly green color scheme. Yellow evokes optimism and warmth but can also cause anxiety if overused. Orange combines the energy of red with the cheerfulness of yellow and is often used to convey a sense of fun and affordability. Brands like Amazon and Nickelodeon use orange to appear approachable and exciting.

The effectiveness of color in marketing depends heavily on context and culture. In Western cultures, white is associated with purity and cleanliness, which is why it dominates packaging for health and hygiene products. In many Asian cultures, however, white is the color of mourning and may have negative associations for some consumers. Similarly, while red is associated with danger and urgency in Western markets, it symbolizes good luck and prosperity in Chinese culture, which is why it features prominently in marketing campaigns targeting Chinese consumers, particularly during the Lunar New Year.

A fascinating area of research concerns the effect of color on taste perception. Studies have shown that the color of food and drink packaging significantly influences how consumers expect the product to taste. In one famous experiment, researchers added tasteless red coloring to a batch of white peach-flavored drinks. Participants who received the red-colored drinks consistently rated them as having a stronger peach flavor than those who received the uncolored white drinks, even though the drinks were identical in every other respect. This demonstrates the powerful role that visual cues play in shaping our sensory experiences.

Color also plays a crucial role in store design and layout. Research has found that warm colors such as red and orange create a sense of stimulation and urgency, encouraging impulse purchases, which is why they are commonly used in fast-food restaurants and discount stores. Cool colors like blue and green create a calming atmosphere that encourages customers to spend more time browsing, which is why luxury retailers and department stores tend to favor these colors. The lighting temperature, whether warm or cool, also affects how colors are perceived under artificial light, a factor that store designers must carefully consider.

title.en: Passage 1 - William Henry Perkin: The Man Who Invented Synthetic Dyes
title.zh: 文章1 - 威廉·亨利·珀金：发明合成染料的人

sections.passage:
The earliest dyes were made from natural materials such as plants, minerals, and insects. Tyrian purple, extracted from a species of sea snail, was so expensive that in ancient Rome only emperors were permitted to wear it. Indigo, derived from the leaves of the indigo plant, was the most widely used blue dye for centuries. However, natural dyes were often expensive, inconsistent in quality, and limited in color range. The development of synthetic dyes in the mid-19th century transformed the textile industry and made colorful clothing accessible to ordinary people for the first time.

The story of synthetic dyes begins with an 18-year-old chemistry student named William Henry Perkin. In 1856, Perkin was working in his home laboratory in London, attempting to synthesize quinine, a treatment for malaria, from coal tar, a cheap byproduct of the gas industry. His experiment failed to produce quinine, but when cleaning his flask with alcohol, he noticed that the residue produced a brilliant purple color. Recognizing the potential of this discovery, Perkin experimented further and found that the substance could be used to dye silk, producing a vivid purple that was remarkably resistant to fading.

Perkin named his discovery mauveine, after the French word for the mallow flower, which has a similar purple color. He quickly patented his invention and, with the financial backing of his father and brother, built a factory at Greenford Green in northwest London to manufacture the dye commercially. The timing was perfect: Queen Victoria wore a silk dress dyed with mauveine to her daughter's wedding in 1858, and the color became an instant fashion sensation. The demand for mauveine was enormous, and Perkin's factory was soon producing it on an industrial scale.

The success of mauveine sparked a wave of research into synthetic dyes derived from coal tar. German chemists, in particular, seized on the opportunity and established a thriving chemical industry based on synthetic dye production. By 1870, Germany had overtaken Britain as the leading producer of synthetic dyes, a position it maintained until the outbreak of World War I. Companies such as BASF, Bayer, and Hoechst, which were founded as dye manufacturers, later diversified into pharmaceuticals and other chemicals and remain major corporations today.

Perkin himself continued to make important contributions to chemistry. In 1868, he achieved the synthesis of alizarin, the red dye previously obtained exclusively from the madder root. This was commercially significant because it demonstrated that the most popular natural dyes could be replicated synthetically, eventually making natural dye production obsolete. Perkin also developed a method for synthesizing coumarin, a fragrant compound used in perfumery.

Despite his groundbreaking achievements, Perkin remained a modest and private individual. He was knighted in 1906, the same year that the Chemical Society held a special celebration to mark the 50th anniversary of his discovery of mauveine. He died a few months later, aged 68. His legacy extends far beyond the purple dye that made him famous: he is widely regarded as the founder of the synthetic organic chemicals industry, which today encompasses pharmaceuticals, plastics, agrochemicals, and many other products that are essential to modern life.

title.en: Passage 2 - Is There Anybody Out There? The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence
title.zh: 文章2 - 外面有人吗？寻找外星智慧生命

sections.passage:
The question of whether we are alone in the universe has fascinated humanity for millennia. In the 20th century, advances in astronomy and technology transformed this ancient philosophical question into a legitimate scientific endeavor known as SETI, the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence. Despite decades of effort and millions of hours of observation, SETI has yet to detect any confirmed signals from alien civilizations. However, the search continues, driven by compelling scientific reasoning and ever-improving technology.

The scientific basis for SETI rests on two key assumptions. First, given that there are an estimated 200 billion trillion stars in the observable universe, and that a significant proportion of these stars are likely to have orbiting planets, the sheer number of potential habitats for life suggests that Earth may not be unique. The discovery of exoplanets, planets orbiting stars other than our Sun, has dramatically strengthened this argument. Since the first confirmed exoplanet detection in 1992, astronomers have identified over 5,000 exoplanets, many of which lie within the so-called habitable zone where liquid water could exist on their surfaces.

Second, SETI assumes that if intelligent life does exist elsewhere, some civilizations may develop technology capable of transmitting detectable electromagnetic signals into space. Radio waves are the most commonly searched-for signals because they travel at the speed of light, can penetrate the interstellar medium with little attenuation, and are relatively easy to detect with large radio telescopes. The logic is straightforward: if we can detect natural radio emissions from distant galaxies, we should theoretically be able to detect artificial signals from a technological civilization, provided those signals are powerful enough.

The modern SETI effort began in 1960 when astronomer Frank Drake conducted Project Ozma, using a 25-meter radio telescope at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory in Green Bank, West Virginia. Drake targeted two nearby Sun-like stars, Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani, listening for radio signals at a frequency of 1,420 megahertz, the natural emission frequency of hydrogen, the most abundant element in the universe. The reasoning was that any technologically sophisticated civilization would likely be aware of this frequency and might choose to use it for interstellar communication. Although Project Ozma detected no alien signals during its two months of observation, it established the methodology that subsequent SETI projects would follow.

The most comprehensive SETI project to date has been the Allen Telescope Array, a set of 42 radio telescopes located at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory in northern California. Funded primarily by Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, the array was designed specifically for SETI research and could simultaneously observe multiple target stars across a wide range of frequencies. However, funding difficulties led to the array being placed on standby in 2011, and it has operated only intermittently since then. The Breakthrough Listen project, launched in 2015 with 100 million dollars in funding from Russian billionaire Yuri Milner, represents the most ambitious and well-funded SETI initiative ever undertaken. Using existing radio telescopes around the world, it aims to survey one million nearby stars and 100 nearby galaxies over a ten-year period.

Critics of SETI raise the Fermi Paradox, first articulated by physicist Enrico Fermi in 1950: if intelligent extraterrestrial life is common, as the vast number of potential habitats suggests, why have we not detected any evidence of it? Possible answers include the possibility that intelligent civilizations tend to self-destruct before achieving interstellar communication, that they choose not to broadcast signals, that the distances between civilizations are simply too vast for signals to have reached us yet, or that advanced civilizations communicate using methods we cannot yet detect. The most humbling possibility is that intelligent life is genuinely rare, perhaps even unique to Earth.

title.zh: 文章3 - 博物馆的发展

sections.passage:
The purpose of the modern museum has been debated since the earliest public collections were established in the 18th century. Traditionally, museums served as repositories of knowledge and culture, preserving important objects for the education and enlightenment of the public. In recent decades, however, museums have increasingly been expected to entertain as well as educate, to attract diverse audiences, and to generate revenue. These changing expectations have transformed the way museums operate and have raised fundamental questions about their role in society.

The earliest museums grew out of the private collections of wealthy individuals. The Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, which opened in 1683, is generally considered the first public museum. It was based on the collection of Elias Ashmole, a wealthy antiquarian who donated his collection of natural history specimens, coins, and curiosities to the University of Oxford. The British Museum, established in 1753, was the first national public museum and was based on the collections of Sir Hans Sloane, a physician and naturalist who bequeathed his vast collection of books, manuscripts, and natural specimens to the nation.

Throughout the 19th century, museums proliferated across Europe and North America. The industrial revolution created a new class of wealthy philanthropists who funded the construction of grand museum buildings and donated their private collections. Museums became symbols of national pride and cultural achievement. The Louvre in Paris, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, and the National Gallery in London were all established or greatly expanded during this period. The prevailing philosophy was that museums should be temples of learning, serious institutions where visitors could contemplate great works of art and learn about the natural world.

The 20th century brought significant changes. The concept of the 'new museology,' which emerged in the 1980s, argued that museums should move away from being object-centered institutions focused on collecting and preserving artifacts, and instead become visitor-centered spaces that prioritize the needs and experiences of their audiences. This philosophy emphasized interactive exhibits, multimedia presentations, and participatory experiences over traditional glass cases and explanatory labels. Science museums and discovery centers led this transformation, with institutions like the Exploratorium in San Francisco, founded in 1969, pioneering hands-on, interactive exhibits that encouraged visitors to learn through direct experimentation.

The digital revolution has further transformed museums. Many institutions now offer virtual tours, online collections, and digital exhibitions that can be accessed from anywhere in the world. The Google Arts and Culture platform, launched in 2011, provides high-resolution images of artworks from over 2,000 museums and cultural institutions worldwide. During the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced the temporary closure of museums around the world, digital engagement became essential for maintaining public access to collections and generating revenue through online ticket sales and virtual programming.

Today's museums face the challenge of balancing multiple roles: they must be educational institutions, tourist attractions, research centers, and community spaces simultaneously. The most successful museums manage to combine scholarly rigor with engaging presentation, preserving the past while making it relevant to contemporary audiences. As museum scholar Stephen Weil famously observed, the modern museum has shifted from being 'about something' to being 'for somebody,' a transformation that reflects broader changes in how we think about the relationship between cultural institutions and the public they serve.
